cleanIntro:
This guide follows Smith & Wesson's book for its modern-style J, K, L and N frame revolvers. Smith & Wesson lists the Model 22 Classic among its N-frame revolvers, but the book never prints the name Model 22 Classic, so check your revolver against the book before you start.

The book publishes no disassembly at all. Cleaning is done with the revolver whole and the cylinder swung out to the left; the side plate, the barrel and the lockwork stay where they are. Every step below carries the book's own words and the page they sit on.

steps.title: Make sure this is the book for your revolver
steps.action: This procedure comes from Smith & Wesson's manual for modern-style J, K, L and N frame revolvers, and the Model 22 Classic is an N-frame. Smith & Wesson publishes separate manuals for two revolvers this book does not cover, the BODYGUARD 38 and the X-FRAME 460 and 500 Magnum, so satisfy yourself you are not holding one of those. Your revolver's model number is stamped inside the yoke, and you can only read it with the cylinder swung open.
steps.prose: The book scopes itself by frame, not by model number, which is why it can cover a whole family of revolvers in one document. Read the number in the yoke once the cylinder is open and empty in the steps below; that is the one place your gun states which model it is.
steps.caution: There are separate manuals for S&W® BODYGUARD® 38 and X-FRAME 460 & 500 Magnum revolvers - available free upon request or via download from our web site.
steps.quote: The internal serial number and the model number appear inside the yoke (FIGURE 3) when the cylinder is in the open position.
steps.cite:
SAFETY & INSTRUCTION MANUAL
Revolvers
- Modern Style - J, K, L and N Frame - — p/n 416560000 REV:S&W_REVOLVER_112119 — Model and Features Identification, p.14

steps.title: Hammer at rest before anything else
steps.action: Point the revolver in a safe direction, finger off the trigger and outside the guard, and look at the hammer. If it is forward at rest, go on. If it is cocked, lower it the way the book describes before you open anything: the thumb of your free hand between the hammer and the frame, the thumb of your firing hand on the hammer spur, a press of the trigger only until the hammer comes out of cock, then finger straight out of the guard and the hammer eased forward to rest.
steps.prose: The finger leaving the guard the instant the hammer moves is the part that protects you: if your thumb slips with the trigger still held back, the revolver fires. If the hammer seems to stop partway down, the book's answer is to thumb it back to full cock with your finger outside the guard and decock again properly.
steps.quote: Make sure your finger is off the trigger and the trigger is in the “at rest” or forward position.
steps.cite:
SAFETY & INSTRUCTION MANUAL
Revolvers
- Modern Style - J, K, L and N Frame - — p/n 416560000 REV:S&W_REVOLVER_112119 — Unloading, p.24
steps.warn: You must always control the hammer with your thumbs when decocking the handgun.

steps.title: If yours has the internal lock, the cylinder tells you nothing
steps.action: Some Model 22 Classics carry Smith & Wesson's internal key lock, just above the thumbpiece on the left side of the frame; some are built without it. If yours has one, know that a locked revolver can still have its cylinder opened and closed, so the lock is no evidence either way about whether the gun is loaded. Clear it exactly as you would an unlocked one.
steps.prose: On a revolver with an exposed hammer the lock shows a flag marked LOCKED when it is engaged. Never test the lock with the trigger: the book forbids it, and if the lock is off the hammer falls.
steps.quote: The position of the cylinder has no relationship to the locked status of the revolver.
steps.cite:
SAFETY & INSTRUCTION MANUAL
Revolvers
- Modern Style - J, K, L and N Frame - — p/n 416560000 REV:S&W_REVOLVER_112119 — Internal Lock Mechanism, p.17
steps.warn: NEVER ATTEMPT TO DETERMINE WHETHER A REVOLVER IS LOCKED OR UNLOCKED BY PULLING THE TRIGGER.

steps.title: Thumbpiece forward, cylinder out to the left
steps.action: With your finger off the trigger and outside the trigger guard and the muzzle in a safe direction, press the thumbpiece fully forward and hold it there, then push the cylinder out to the left. Check that every charge hole is free of live ammunition and that the bore is clear of obstructions.
steps.prose: Hold the thumbpiece forward until the cylinder is moving rather than tapping it, or the cylinder will not come out of the frame. Charge holes and bore are two separate checks and the book asks for both: an empty cylinder tells you nothing about what is sitting in the barrel.
steps.quote: You must verify that all charge holes (chambers) are free of live ammunition and that the bore is free of obstructions.
steps.cite:
SAFETY & INSTRUCTION MANUAL
Revolvers
- Modern Style - J, K, L and N Frame - — p/n 416560000 REV:S&W_REVOLVER_112119 — Inspecting Your Revolver, p.15
steps.warn: Always make sure the revolver is unloaded before you inspect or clean it, and keep the muzzle pointed in a safe direction throughout.

steps.title: Muzzle up, extractor rod through, then count
steps.action: Hold the cylinder fully out, point the barrel upward in a safe direction and press the extractor rod through the cylinder so everything lifts clear. Rounds or cases fired in a moon clip come out still held in the clip, so lift the whole clip away. Take everything out of the gun and count it against the six charge holes.
steps.prose: Muzzle up is the whole trick: with the barrel down, a case that only lifts partway slides back into its hole and reads as an empty chamber from the front. A moon clip hides a missing round well, so count the cartridges in the clip as well as the clips themselves.
steps.caution: Carefully count the cartridges or spent casings to be sure that you have recovered all of them.
steps.quote: With the barrel pointing upward in a safe direction, press the extractor rod through the cylinder and remove all cartridges or casings from the cylinder
steps.cite:
SAFETY & INSTRUCTION MANUAL
Revolvers
- Modern Style - J, K, L and N Frame - — p/n 416560000 REV:S&W_REVOLVER_112119 — Unloading, p.24

steps.title: Read the barrel, and 45 ACP only in a moon clip
steps.action: The cartridge designation marked on the barrel is the instruction for what goes in this cylinder. If your revolver is chambered for a rimless cartridge such as 45 ACP, those rounds go in only held in a moon clip. Nothing marked +P+, and no reloaded or handloaded ammunition that has not been pressure-tested.
steps.prose: A rimless case has nothing of its own to stop it at the right depth in a revolver chamber or for the extractor to push against; the clip does both jobs. A cartridge the barrel does not name may still fit a chamber, and fitting is not permission.
steps.caution: “Plus-P-Plus” (+P+) ammunition must not be used in Smith & Wesson firearms.
steps.quote: If your Smith & Wesson revolver is chambered to accept a rimless cartridge such as 45 ACP or 38 Super, a “moon clip” must be used to ensure proper headspacing and extraction of the cartridge.
steps.cite:
SAFETY & INSTRUCTION MANUAL
Revolvers
- Modern Style - J, K, L and N Frame - — p/n 416560000 REV:S&W_REVOLVER_112119 — Use of Moon Clips in Some S&W Revolvers, p.28

steps.title: Field strip complete
steps.action: An open, empty cylinder is the whole of it. Smith & Wesson publishes no disassembly procedure for this revolver: the cylinder, yoke, extractor, hammer and lockwork all stay in the frame and the side plate stays on. Everything the cleaning below asks for is reachable through the open cylinder.
steps.prose: The book's caution points you at the Field Stripping and Inspection sections, and this book has an Inspection section and no Field Stripping section at all. For this revolver that is the answer, not an omission: there is nothing to strip.
steps.quote: Never disassemble your firearm beyond the instructions in the Field Stripping and Inspection sections of this manual.
steps.cite:
SAFETY & INSTRUCTION MANUAL
Revolvers
- Modern Style - J, K, L and N Frame - — p/n 416560000 REV:S&W_REVOLVER_112119 — Cleaning and Maintenance, p.30

deepAbsentReason: There is no deep clean in the J, K, L and N frame book this guide follows. Its table of contents (printed p.3) has no field-stripping or disassembly section, and its cleaning pages (printed pp.30-32) work with the revolver whole. The book sends any maintenance or service it does not describe to a qualified gunsmith using genuine Smith & Wesson parts (printed p.31), and a revolver showing wear back to Smith & Wesson or a qualified gunsmith (printed p.32).

cleaning.name: BORE AND CHARGE HOLES
tasks: Before the first shooting, wipe the factory preservative or oil from the bore, the charge holes and the exposed areas with a clean swab or patch
Remove excessive firing residue from the bore and every charge hole with a properly fitted brass brush dipped in gun cleaning solvent
Finish with a dry cotton patch through the bore and each charge hole to carry the residue and solvent back out
Use cleaning supplies made for your caliber, and a cleaning rod long enough to push the brush and jag all the way through the barrel

cleaning.name: MOON CLIPS
tasks: Pull each case straight out of the clip toward its opening; on a full moon clip, pry the first one out and the rest come easier
Inspect every moon clip after each use
Do not reuse a clip that is broken, bent or cracked: discard it and replace it with a straight, new one

cleaning.name: EXTERIOR, LUBRICATION AND STORAGE
tasks: Clean the exterior with a non-abrasive cloth and take off every trace of cleaning solution, oil and fingerprints; finger moisture left on the metal can start corrosion
Do not use ammoniated or other strong alkaline solvents on a Smith & Wesson, and avoid prolonged solvent soaking and prolonged ultrasonic cleaning
After cleaning, lightly coat the metal parts, inside and out, with a high quality gun oil
In a cold climate, choose an oil weight that will not congeal and slow the action
After exposure to sand, dust, extreme humidity or water, clean and lubricate the revolver before it is put away

For long storage, oil the bore, charge holes and internal mechanism and coat the outside and barrel with an anti-rust oil; do not store it in leather or heavy cloth, and never with a plug in the barrel
Check for signs of wear every time you clean. If you find wear, do not use the revolver: return it to Smith & Wesson for service or have it checked by a qualified gunsmith

reassembly: Nothing came off the revolver, so there is nothing to rebuild. Push the cylinder back into the frame until it locks into place; press it home rather than flicking it shut.
Turn the closed cylinder gently by hand until it stops in line, so you know it is locked.
Before the revolver is used again, run a clean patch through the bore and each charge hole to take out oil left there by the cleaning.
fncheck: With every charge hole confirmed empty and the bore clear, close the cylinder and check that it locks into place and that pressing the thumbpiece forward lets it swing out again cleanly. Still empty and pointed in a safe direction, cock the hammer and practise the book's decocking procedure, thumbs controlling the hammer, until it returns all the way to its at-rest position. If your revolver has the internal lock, the key turns about 90 degrees each way with a definite stop and detent, and the LOCKED flag shows only when it is locked; never test it with the trigger.
